It summarizes the teachings of Vedānta as follows: Among the three ultimate entities recognized by philosophy, the intelligent individual soul is essentially...
It is distinct from insentient matter and the supreme Brahman. Thus, the essential differences existing between matter,

God, by means of His subtle body, constitutes the universe in His causal state; and by means of His gross body, He forms the created universe itself. As for the individual souls...
Just as a person enters into matter and thereby brings it to life,
so too does God enter into matter and the soul, bestowing upon them their respective powers and specific characteristics. The universe...
To be without God is precisely analogous to matter without a soul; and in the world as we know it, all things are what they are because God has penetrated into them.
And He rules and guides them all from within, such that all things are His representatives and all words primarily denote Him.

The scripture, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," briefly states what is to be attended to by those seeking liberation: the supreme reality, the beneficial, and the human goal. The supreme reality is Brahman; knowledge of It is the benefit; and the attainment of It is the human goal. Having thus indicated these very points in brief, he himself explains them with some detail.

"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. He who knows it as hidden in the secret cave of the heart, in the highest heaven—he, together with the all-knowing Brahman, attains all desires. Thus, [Brahman] is endowed with existence that is free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhika-sattā*).

The nature of Brahman has been explained as being of the single form of eternally uncontracted knowledge, devoid of the three kinds of limitations. It is stated that meditation is beneficial by means of the term "knowledge" characterized by its being situated within the cave of the heart. In the supreme abode, designated as the non-material ether, there is the experience of the Supreme Brahman, distinguished by all auspicious qualities; this is the highest—

And this has been explained as the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*). For instance, in the passage, “He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman,” the phrase “in the supreme ether” refers to the supreme state (*paramapada*), which is designated by the term ‘ether’ as being non-material (*aprākṛta*).
It is preceded by the attainment of that specific location known as the supreme state, which is non-material, and [it consists in the enjoyment] of the Supreme Brahman and its attributes.

It is thus stated that the complete experience itself is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Nor should it be suspected that there is a contradiction with the term "infinite" (*ananta*), which establishes the absence of the three kinds of limitation, on the grounds that Brahman is spatially limited by its existence in a specific location called the "supreme abode" (*paramapada*); for we do not [assert] that Brahman exists elsewhere than in the supreme abode because of the statement regarding its being situated therein.
We shall set aside [the notion of] spatial limitation, such that there would be a contradiction; rather, [it is as stated in the scriptures]: "He who knows...
who has entered within, the ruler of people, the Self of all," and "eternal..."
"I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, seated in the heart of all beings" (Gītā 10.20);

"Viṣṇu is omnipresent"; "because of the omnipresence of the Infinite"—by hundreds of such authorities, He has been described as the inner Self of all and as being omnipresent; yet, [He is here spoken of] as characterized by His divine and auspicious form, eternally...

And we speak of the Lord’s abiding in a particular location on account of His possession of manifold glory (vibhūti). For scriptural passages such as, “Dwelling in the far distance of this space” and “That is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu,” establish that even though Brahman is omnipresent, He resides in specific locations.
"The pervasive, omnipresent [Self] is hidden in the cave"; and thus, attainment— which consists of direct experience— is obtained, as is the supreme Brahman, the object to be attained.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that this lay follower (*upāsaka*) enjoys all desires together with *brahman*. Here, in the phrase "together with *brahman*," the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*), according to the grammatical rule "when joined with *saha*, the subordinate [element takes the third case]. And this [instrumental] refers to the accompaniment of the object of enjoyment (*bhogya-sāhitya*), as in the example "he eats rice with milk. Thus, [the meaning is] "those [desires] accompanied by *brahman*."

The meaning is that he enjoys all desires; however, it does not mean "being accompanied by Brahman, like a father who has come with his son," where the intent would be on the accompaniment of the enjoyer, for in that case, it would follow that Brahman is not the primary subject. Even if it were intended as an accompaniment of the object of enjoyment, [the primacy of Brahman remains].
The argument that "the lack of predominance is equal" finds its application in the maxim, "And when a defect is equal for both sides.

Nevertheless, that lack of predominance, by demonstrating the excellence of the enjoyability of His multitude of qualities, culminates in the preeminence of Brahman; thus, it does not constitute a fault, but rather serves as a merit. This is like the brilliance of gems—
For the presentation of the bed culminates in the excellence of the jewels. As it has been said by the learned:

"We declare that glory here to be even higher than yours; listen well! Alternatively, just as in the Dahara-vidyā, the word "together" (saha) is used here to indicate that the qualities are objects of enjoyment.

The word "saha" (together) is used for the purpose of stating this. Here, by establishing that the attributes of Brahman are objects of enjoyment in liberation, it is determined that even the meditation which serves as the means belongs to Brahman with attributes alone, according to the principle of *tatkratu* (as one intends in one's meditation, so one becomes). If Brahman were devoid of distinctions, then meditation upon it would consist in its non-difference from the inner self (*pratyag-ātman*).

If that were intended to be explained, then in the Śruti there would be a statement regarding the enjoyability of the inner self (pratyagātman) and the absence of those qualities [in it], but not regarding Brahman and its qualities; this is how it should be understood. XXIX It might be argued as follows:

For the *tatkratu-nyāya* (the principle that the result corresponds to the intention) establishes the necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of those attributes (*dharmas*) contemplated during the stage of the means (*upāyadaśā*) with the stage of the goal (*upeyadaśā*); it does not, however, state the exclusion of additional attributes therein.
As stated by the venerable Teacher:

"That non-exclusion [of qualities] even when [the primary goal] has been attained— which belongs to one who has worshipped [the Lord] as possessing those qualities— is to be understood through the principle of *tatkratu* (as one intends, so one becomes), and not as the exclusion of other forms. Otherwise, if liberation were [attained] through worship characterized by only a few qualities specifically prescribed for a particular knowledge (*vidyā*), [there would be a contradiction].

There would be no experience of the complete Brahman; for the experience of the complete Brahman is indeed taught as the experience of Brahman characterized by all attributes, in the passage: "All desires together with Brahman. Therefore, even in the meditation upon the attributeless Brahman, the experience of the qualities of Brahman at the time of the attainment of the fruit is not contradictory. As for that which is non-different from the inner self—

The claim that the experience of Brahman during meditation is not appropriate for the state of fruition is also incorrect; for it is precisely the experience of Brahman as non-different from the inner self (*pratyag-ātman*) that is taught by the Śruti in the words, "by the wise Brahman" (*brahmaṇā vipaścitā*).

To explain: the instrumental case in "by Brahman" (*brahmaṇā*) is not used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*), because the word "Brahman" cannot logically be construed with another in a relationship of accompaniment.

The word *saha* (together) establishes simultaneity in the enjoyment of all desires by attaining the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) "he enjoys all desires together. The term *brahmaṇā* means "having become Brahman. Being himself one who has become Brahman, the worshiper enjoys all desires simultaneously, and not as in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
"Gradually"—thus, there is not even a scent of fault.

To this it is replied: if one maintains that through the meditation on Brahman without attributes there is an experience of qualities at the stage of the attainment of the fruit, then the contradiction with the *tatkratu-nyāya* (the principle that "as one intends, so one becomes") is insurmountable. Furthermore, the resolution of this contradiction according to the method stated by the venerable Teacher (Sureśvara) does not apply here.

He proceeds: although the experience of another form that is not contradictory to the qualities [previously] cultivated may be logically possible, the experience of a form contradictory to those is simply impossible. For being possessed of attributes (*saviśeṣatva*) is contradicted by being without attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*).

Furthermore, regarding the gloss on the word "by Brahman" (*brahmaṇā*) as "having become Brahman" (*brahmabhūta*), it is considered there: the word "by Brahman" is in the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*).

How can there be an explanation of the meaning of the word *anta* when it ends in the nominative case? The instrumental case, which would naturally arise in connection with a companion (*sahayoga*), has been set aside. Upon examining the method of exposition in the phrase "become Brahman" (*brahmabhūta*), it appears that the instrumental case intended here is that used for a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe*).
However, that [usage] is not applicable here; for that [instrumental] is prescribed after a word expressing a characteristic mark of something already so constituted.

As in the example "the ascetic by means of matted hair" (*jaṭābhis tāpasaḥ*), such a possibility does not exist here. For while the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is prescribed after words such as *prakṛti* (in the sense of "instrument"), it would apply here only if a general relation were intended; since that is absent in the present context, the third case does not apply.

Furthermore, a relation termed "non-difference" (*abhedākhya*) is not accepted [as a basis for the third case]; otherwise, in examples such as "the blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*), [the same error would follow].

If it were a general relation in the absence of distinction, the undesirable application of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would be unavoidable. However, it should be understood that there is no occasion for such a doubt here, because the Vārttika— "An addition [to the rule] regarding *prakṛti* and so forth"— has been rejected in the original treatise (*ākara*).
Thus, when the principles, the beneficial, and the human goals proclaimed in the Vedānta were being thrown into confusion by various adventitious [doctrines],

the Lord Nārāyaṇa, intent on the protection of Dharma, descended in the form of Bādarāyaṇa and composed the four-chaptered Brahma-mīmāṃsā in order to properly establish the principles, the beneficial, and the human goals that are not [found] in other Upaniṣads. This very [work]—

Mīmāṃsā, by expounding through its four chapters the topics of reconciliation (*samanvaya*), non-contradiction (*avirodha*), means (*sādhana*), and fruit (*phala*), becomes the procedural requirement (*itikartavyatā*) for the realization of Brahman. As they have said:
"But when the Supreme Self is being known through the Vedāntas as the instruments..."
The wise know this Uttara-mīmāṃsā to be the prescribed procedure [for that realization].

Thus [it is said]. The subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this treatise is Brahman and its meditations (*upāsanā*) and so forth. Its fruit (*phala*) is the definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) thereof. This is because the term "Brahman" is employed in the scriptural passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," as well as at the commencement of the treatise in the statement, "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*). Thus, the Brahman that is sought to be known is [defined] by its essential nature (*svarūpa*), its forms (*rūpa*), its qualities (*guṇa*), its manifestations (*vibhava*), and so on, which are beyond [limitation].

It is understood as "cut. For the word *brahman* is derived from the verbal root *bṛh* (or *bṛhi*), meaning "to grow" or "to increase," and it expresses the unsurpassed greatness of Brahman both in its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and in its qualities (*guṇa*). Accordingly, there is this etymological definition:
"Why is it called *brahman*? Because great (*bṛhantaḥ*) indeed are the qualities within it"; and "Because it grows (*bṛhati*) and causes to grow (*bṛṃhayati*), therefore..."
It is said: "The Supreme Brahman"; and, "Because of its vastness (*bṛhat*) and because of its expanding nature (*bṛṃhaṇa*), it is designated as Brahman.
Having thus meditated upon Brahman, the venerable Śruti proceeds to define it in detail:
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone; one only, without a second"; and, "All this has that as its self."
"xxxii.
By such statements as 'All this is what this Self is' and 'There is no diversity whatsoever here,' [the identity] of Brahman..."

Having declared that *sattva* is oneness and non-duality, [the scripture] teaches that the entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is of the nature of Brahman; thus, it negates the existence of a world that is separate from or diverse from Brahman. Likewise, there are such passages as: "Partless, actionless, tranquil, irreproachable, stainless," and "devoid of qualities."
The Śrutis establish that Brahman is partless (*niravayavatva*), actionless (*niṣkriyatva*), and devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*).

Thus, because the Śrutis demonstrate the non-existence of the world as distinct from Brahman, and because they establish Brahman’s qualitylessness, actionlessness, and so forth, it is understood that Brahman is without distinction (*nirviśeṣa*). Furthermore, the world has this as its self (*aitadātmyam*).

That which is being propounded results in the negation of the world; just as in the cases "the snake is identical with the rope" and "the silver is identical with the mother-of-pearl," the identity with the rope and the identity with the mother-of-pearl, when predicated of the snake and the silver, result in the negation of the snake and the silver. And therefore, the "one only, without a second" taught in the Śruti—this "one"— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument presented.]
At first glance, it appears that the non-duality and attributelessness of Brahman are being taught;

however, this is countered by such scriptural passages as: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge," "His desires are true, His resolves are true," and "His power is indeed manifold, heard of as innate, as well as His knowledge, strength, and action."

Because Brahman is understood to possess distinctions through such supporting texts as, “A unique mass of qualities such as splendor, strength, sovereignty, great awakening, excellent heroism, and power,” and “Although You possess infinite qualities, these six are Your primary qualities,” it is understood that the previously mentioned oneness and non-duality belong to Brahman as qualified by attributes (*saviśeṣa-brahma*). Therefore, non-duality is [not absolute].
Whether it be "non-duality of the remainder" (*śeṣādvaita*) or "non-duality with attributes" (*saviśeṣādvaita*), duality has emerged within non-duality itself; this is indeed a great diversity.

Regarding this, what do the scriptures establish there—is it the non-dual Brahman without attributes (*nirviśeṣabrahmādvaita*), or rather the non-dual Brahman with attributes (*saviśeṣabrahmādvaita*)?

Now is the occasion for an inquiry into duality. In that regard, it is understood that the purport of the Śruti texts lies in the non-duality of Brahman with attributes (*saviśeṣa-brahmādvaita*), and not in the non-duality of Brahman without attributes (*nirviśeṣa-brahmādvaita*). For instance, the Vedāntas explicitly designate three principles—the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*), the principle of unconsciousness (*acittattva*), and the principle of Brahman (*brahmatattva*)—and demonstrate the mutual distinction between these principles.

And they clarify their mutual relationship. Therefore, just like the reality of Brahman, neither the reality of consciousness nor the reality of the non-conscious can be denied by anyone. Likewise, the mutual relationship between these three realities, being established by uncontradicted means of valid cognition, is not subject to denial. As stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:
"66xxxii This Lord sustains the entire universe—the perishable and the imperishable, the manifest and the unmanifest—joined together.
Yet the self, though not the Lord, is bound by the state of being an enjoyer; by knowing the God, one is released from all fetters."

Thus, there are three principles: the perishable (kṣara), the imperishable (akṣara), and the Lord (īśa). Here, the unmanifest (avyakta) principle is called the "perishable" because it is subject to decay and because it undergoes transformation into a gross form through the differentiation of name and form; it is also called the "manifest" (vyakta). The manifest principle, which is the category of individual souls (jīva), is called the "imperishable" because it is not subject to decay and exists in a subtle form.

The Lord, the Supreme Self, sustains the manifest perishable aggregate of non-consciousness (*acid-varga*) and the unmanifest imperishable aggregate of consciousness (*cid-varga*), joined together and mutually blended. The meaning is that He sustains the pure aggregate of non-consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, and likewise the aggregate of beings joined with one another. As it has been said: "Being the sustainer, while being sustained Himself, He sustains [all]" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.17); and "He who [sustains] the three worlds... (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.13.2).

"Entering [them], the immutable Lord sustains [them]. For here, by the term "the three worlds," the triad consisting of the insentient, the sentient bound [to it], and the liberated is expressed. And their "sustenance" consists in the maintenance of their essential nature, existence, and activity by virtue of His being their inner self (*antarātman*). Even while being thus [the sustainer], He is not bound; for He is not subject to [the power of] *niyati*.

The individual soul (*jīva*), however, is bound because it is the experiencer of the fruits of karma. But for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), since all desires have been attained, there is no longing for the fruits of karma; therefore, there is no possibility of bondage. As it has been said:
"Actions do not taint Me, nor do I have any longing for the fruits of action. Thus [is] the Lord, the God...

"He who knows [the Self] by way of its distinction from the conscious and the unconscious is liberated from all fetters; he becomes released from all bonds"—thus it is stated that the knowledge of the distinction between the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord is the cause of liberation. Likewise:
The two unborn ones—the Knower and the Unknower—are the Lord and the Non-Lord; the one unborn [nature] is joined with the enjoyer and the objects of enjoyment.
When one perceives this triad as the infinite Self, whose form is the universe and who is indeed a non-doer, that is Brahman.

Between the two—the Supreme and the individual soul—mentioned in the preceding statement, one is the Lord (*īśa*): omniscient and the controller; the other is ignorant, not the Lord, and the controlled. However, the absence of birth is common to both. In the term *īśanīśau*, the absence of the *savarṇadīrgha* (lengthening of similar vowels) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Its meaning is *īśānīśau*. Alternatively, it may be analyzed as *īṃṭū* and *anīṭ*.

And in the phrase *īśānīśau*, the absence of the *jaśtva* substitution is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). The nature of the non-conscious principle (*acittattva*) is now elaborated: "For there is one unborn [female]" (*ajā hyekā*). This means that the "unborn" (*ajā*)—referring to *prakṛti* (Nature)—is distinct from the two others, possesses the purposeful activity of providing enjoyment for the enjoyer, the individual soul (*jīva*), and is devoid of birth (*utpatti-rahitā*). Thus, although these three principles are equal in being devoid of birth, [the Lord is distinguished] by His omniscience...

The meaning is that [the two] are mutually distinct by virtue of attributes such as omniscience and insentience. The absence of bondage in the Supreme Self is stated by the words "eternal" (ananta) and so forth. Although the Supreme Self has the universe as His body, He is the locus of infinite qualities such as the possession of true desires; therefore, He is independent. Consequently, unlike the individual soul (jīva), He does not act preceded by an expectation of results.

[The Self] possesses agency; therefore, the sense is that Prakṛti does not exist for the sake of its enjoyment. He states the fruit of such knowledge of the mutual distinction between the two: "When one knows the triad... When one knows these three principles as mutually distinct, then one becomes Brahman; because of the abandonment of material name and form, [one is] freed from what is produced by them.

The meaning of "difference" (*bheda*) is that, by virtue of having the single form of knowledge, [the individual soul] becomes similar to Brahman and is denoted by the word "Brahman. Furthermore, the conventional usage of identity (*tattā*) is frequently observed when there is a unity of mode, as in the expression, "This is that very rice. However, the intended meaning here is not the non-difference (*abheda*) from Brahman, because difference was previously described in this very context; for it is said, "That which is more numerous shall be stronger."

Because, according to logic, the scriptural texts concerning difference possess greater authority; such scriptural passages are to be understood in this manner. Likewise, there are also corroborative statements (*upabṛṃhaṇa*):
"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, and intellect..."
This eightfold nature of mine, known as egoism, is thus divided.
"O mighty-armed one, know that this is My lower nature; but other than this, know My higher nature, which is of the character of the individual soul (jīva), by which this world is sustained.
Herein, there is the insentient nature consisting of earth and so forth, the sentient nature called the individual soul, and the reality of the Lord who is the substratum of both.

The three principles and their mutual distinction have been pointed out. For here, by the word "me" (*mama*), the Blessed One designates the Self as the sovereign over both the conscious and the unconscious. Therefore, there is a mutual distinction between the conscious and the unconscious based on their respective states of being superior and inferior; and there is a distinction between the conscious and the unconscious and the Lord based on their respective states of being subordinate and sovereign.
It is thus declared:
"Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable, therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). xxxiv
"There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable.
All beings are the perishable; the one who stands firm is called the imperishable."
But there is another, the Supreme Person, who is declared to be the Supreme Self;
the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them.

Thus, because they are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the two principles known as the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*)— just like the principle of God (*īśvara*)— are likewise impossible to deny. Likewise, since the mutual distinctness of these principles is also established by valid means of knowledge,
their difference (*bheda*) is also impossible to deny.
Likewise:
"For him, no effect or instrument is found; neither his equal nor his superior is seen.
His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, and his knowledge, strength, and action are innate."

Thus, in this context, the infinite qualities of the Lord—such as knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor—are heard in scripture. Of that Lord of all, who was previously designated in the preceding mantra as "the supreme Great Lord among lords," there exists neither a body as an effect, nor instruments in the form of sense organs; [there is] no material body.

The meaning is that his ordinary sense organs do not exist. Thus it has been said: "His material form does not consist of flesh, fat, or bone"; and "The body of this Supreme Self is not composed of an aggregate of elements.
Neither one equal to Him nor one superior to Him is seen anywhere in the world. His power—

Accompanied by knowledge and power, the activity characterized by creation, dissolution, and so forth—supreme, distinct from others, manifold, of many kinds, innate, and unconditioned—is heard [in scripture]; that is to say, it is propounded many times in the Śrutis. Likewise:
"One God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings;
the overseer of actions, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, solitary, and devoid of qualities.
"He is the creator of the universe, the knower of the universe, whose source is the Self; he is the master of time, possessed of attributes, and the knower of all sciences."
"The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas, the cause of the bondage, maintenance, and liberation from saṃsāra.

(III.35) He is the Lord (Īśa), the maker of the universe, the creator of all. He is the knower of the universe (Viśvavit); the root *vid* here has the sense of "attainment. The meaning is that he has attained all his desires. Since omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) will be stated immediately thereafter by the word *jña*, [it follows that]—

This is the meaning here: *ātmayoni* means that whose womb or place (*yoni*) is the self (*ātman*), namely the individual soul (*jīva*); the sense is that he is the inner ruler (*antaryāmī*) of the individual soul.
*Svayaṃbhū* means "self-existent," or alternatively, "unborn" (*aja*). He is called *jña* because he knows; the sense is "all-knowing.
The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule "igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ. He is the "time of time" (*kālakāla*), [meaning] even of time...
He is the director. One should reflect on such passages as: "There He ripens time; indeed, time is not the master there.
He is the possessor of qualities (guṇin), being fully endowed with auspicious qualities such as knowledge and power. He is all-knowing (sarvavidya), the impeller of all branches of knowledge.
Or, following the manner stated as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," the word may be divided as *sarvavit* (all-perceiving).

He is the Lord (*pati*), the Sovereign (*śeṣin*) of both Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña—that is, of Prakṛti and Jīva, or the sentient and the insentient. He is the Lord of Qualities (*guṇeśa*), for he rules over everything by means of qualities such as knowledge and power. [Of] Saṃsāra...
The meaning is that [the Lord] is the cause of liberation, which consists in abiding in Him, and of bondage.

As it is said, "The fear of those who enjoy [Him], yet have disregarded Him," the meaning is that He ordains liberation for those who have surrendered (prapanna) and bondage for others. Here too, the infinite qualities of the Blessed One are described.
Fearlessness is relevant here in connection with the primary texts, as well as in the supplementary works (upabṛṃhaṇas).
He is the embodiment of all auspicious qualities; by a mere fraction of His own power, He brings forth the multitude of beings.
Having assumed vast bodies at will according to His desire, He has accomplished the welfare of the entire world.
He is the sole mass of qualities such as splendor, power, sovereignty, great awakening, and heroic strength;
he is the supreme among the supreme, the Lord of the high and the low, in whom no afflictions whatsoever exist.
In such passages as these, qualities such as the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and others belonging to the Supreme Brahman are expounded.

Likewise, the Śrutis establish the relationship between the Supreme Brahman—which is a great ocean of infinite auspicious qualities—and the sentient and insentient entities (*cidacit*) by way of the body-soul (*śarīrātma-bhāva*) relation. For instance, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "He who [dwells] within the earth... [and so forth].

Beginning with "Dwelling," [the text says]: "He who dwells in consciousness, yet is within consciousness, whom consciousness does not know, whose body is consciousness, who controls consciousness from within— he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal."

Thus, here, by the passage beginning with "He who dwells in the earth," the fact that insentient things are presided over by the Blessed One and constitute His body is stated; and by the passage beginning with "He who dwells in the intellect," the fact that individual souls are presided over by the Blessed One and constitute His body is likewise stated, as is the abiding of the Supreme Self within the earth and other elements.
He shows this by saying, "as the inner self of each," and further, "the inner one of the earth, the inner one of consciousness.
By the statement "the inner one governs," the all-pervasive definition of a body is expressed. By this it is meant:
that for which a conscious being is able, in its entirety, to govern and sustain a substance for its own purpose.
And since its sole essential nature consists in being subservient to Him, the definition of a body—that it is "His body"—is established.

Because both sentient and insentient beings can be controlled and sustained by the Lord for His own purposes in every respect, and because their very nature is solely to be subservient to Him, their status as the Lord's body is unassailable. He who dwells within the earth... [tadantarā-]
Being of that very nature, existing within it, unknowable by it, and having it as its body, he exercises control over it;

this is the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), your immortal Self—the meaning being that the Self possesses immortality free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Here, because of the use of the genitive case of separation in the phrase "your Self" (*te ātmā*), the distinction of the Inner Controller from the individual soul (jīva) is established.

One should not suspect that this designation is merely figurative—like the expression "the body of a stone statue"—because, in the absence of any sublation (apavāda), it is impossible to assume that a genitive case used in a sense of distinction (*vyatireka*) is figurative;
furthermore, a genitive denoting non-difference is not accepted by grammarians. Moreover, distinction is established even from the qualification "immortality" (*amṛtatva*).

It is established. When it is said, "The inner controller (*antaryāmī*) is your self (*ātman*)," the exclusion of the individual soul (*jīva*) would not occur because of the suspicion that the word *ātman* refers merely to one's own nature (*svarūpa*); therefore, the term "immortal" (*amṛta*) is stated. This should be understood in the same way for passages such as "He who dwells in consciousness" (*yo vijñāne*). In this very Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa, it says: "He who dwells in consciousness... (*yo vijñāne tiṣṭhan*).

In place of the word *vijñāna* found in the Kāṇva recension, the followers of the Mādhyandina branch read, "He who dwells in the self" (*ya ātmani tiṣṭhan*). Therefore, it is understood that here the word *vijñāna* refers to the individual soul (*jīvātman*).

[The term is derived] as *vijñāna* because it cognizes (*vijānāti*), with the suffix *lyu* (ana) in the sense of the agent according to the rule for roots beginning with *nandi*. Alternatively, it is self-luminous—
Therefore, the designation of "consciousness" (vijñāna) applies to the individual soul (jīva) as well.

Likewise, beginning with: "He who moves within the earth, whose body is the earth, whom the earth does not know," and continuing up to: "He who moves within the Imperishable (akṣara), whose body is the Imperishable, whom the Imperishable does not [know]... [the same logic applies].

The Veda declares elsewhere as well that the individual soul (jīva) has the Supreme Self as its body: "Having created that, He entered into it. Having entered it, He became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat). Thus, preceded by the creation of the world, the scripture teaches that Brahman pervades everything and has everything as its body through its omnipresence.

If it is asked, "What indeed is this so-called 'entry' (anupraveśa) of Brahman, who is all-pervading at all times, at the time of creation?"—to this they reply: Just as a calf exists within the belly of a cow, the "entry" here is simply a specific mode of existence of the all-pervading Brahman within each and every object, such that it is capable of being fully perceived. By this [it is shown that] "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite."
Thus, the statement that Brahman— which was described as being "unlimited"— is "hidden in the cave," as in the passage "He who knows [Brahman] hidden in the cave," is also thereby justified.
Therefore, the Supreme Brahman, which is established by means of valid cognition such as the Śruti, possesses a body consisting of both consciousness (cit) and unconscious matter (acit).

The established doctrine of the Viśiṣṭādvaitins is that the aforementioned scriptural statements are intended to establish qualified non-duality (*saviśeṣādvaita*)— as they result in the realization of [Brahman] as characterized by specific attributes such as being the inner controller of all, having true desires, having true resolves, and possessing unsurpassed sixfold divinity (*ṣāḍguṇya*)— and not unqualified non-duality (*nirviśeṣādvaita*).
Thus, because it intends to convey the non-duality of Brahman as qualified (*saviśeṣa-brahmādvaita*), it is designated as "qualified non-dualism" (*viśiṣṭādvaita*).
This is the underlying idea: the designation is made with the intention of emphasizing that Brahman alone is the single reality (*tattva*) by way of its specific qualification;

however, in its ultimate analysis, there are indeed three principles. Relying upon the doctrine established in its own system (*pratitantra-siddhānta*)—namely, the relationship between the body and the embodied—the distinction [between the individual soul and Brahman]...

The scriptural texts concerning non-difference and those concerning difference can both be established in a state of consistency. Otherwise, one would have to describe the establishment of the difference-texts by resorting to an imagined difference. They maintain that such a description of their establishment would amount to the assumption of the invalidity of those very scriptures.

Relying precisely upon this established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the Blessed Commentator has explained the *Brahmasūtras* in the *Vedāntasāra*. As for the summary of the meaning of the chapters and sections, it has been provided by the authors of that work in their English introduction; therefore, I shall desist from further elaboration here.

"The celestial divine chariots moving without restraint, the assembly halls, the pleasure groves of various kinds, and the lotus ponds..."
"Crystal water— all these, my dear, are hells when compared with that abode of the Supreme Self" (Śaṅkara on Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.9–10). However,
he is an *ativādin* who makes a supreme declaration by means of [the aforementioned knowledge].

"of the Truth" (Chānd. III.16). That he is an *ativādin* is consistent only in this way; for being an *ativādin* means one who speaks of the superiority of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) of his own object of worship.

"You" [refers to the individual soul]. That [bliss] is called "Bhūman" (the Infinite) because it possesses a vastness of the nature described—that is, it is characterized by a magnitude that has "the small" as its counter-correlative.

This one designated by the word "Bhūman" is the Supreme Self, because of the instruction given subsequent to the state of serene composure (*saṃprasāda*). Serene composure is the inner self (*pratyagātman*).
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "Now, he who is this serene being," and because he is taught as something distinct from the inner self—
which was indicated by the word "prāṇa" in the passage beginning, "But he indeed speaks surpassingly who speaks with truth"— as being superior to it.
And because of the logical consistency of the doctrine. || 8 ||
This can reasonably be maintained only by accepting this fact. An *ativādin* (one who speaks "highly") is one who speaks of his object of devotion as being of great benefit.
The word *bhīman*— the antonym of "small"— speaks of the abundance of bliss possessed by Him,
as described above. What is signified by this word...
Bhūman is the Highest Self, because Bhūman is said to be greater than the individual self. The term *samprasāda* occurring in the Sūtra refers to the individual self.
The scriptural text is as follows: "Then this is the individual self (samprasāda)" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4). Consider also the text: "But he is an ativādin who makes [the Self] the supreme..."
The declaration by means of the Truth (Chāndogya Upaniṣad III.16). What is taught here is the Person who is distinct from and superior to the individual self denoted by the word *prāṇa*.
8. And on account of the attributes being suitable [to the Highest Self].
1. Expressing its own nature (*svarūpavācin*): as taught in passages such as *Vedāntasāra*, adhi.
"In what, O Venerable One, is He established? In His own glory," and so forth.

Furthermore, because attributes such as being established in one's own majesty, being the cause of all, and being the self of all are logically possible only in the Supreme, the "Plenum" (bhūman) is the Supreme.
Section on the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa) 3: The Imperishable [is Brahman], because it supports everything up to the ether. 9.

"That which is this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas declare to be neither gross nor subtle"—by such statements, the Imperishable is declared to be the Supreme Brahman, because it is the support of everything up to the ether. Starting from "That, O Gārgī, which is above the sky," [the text continues]: "On what, O Venerable Sir, does that rest? It rests on its own greatness."
"His own greatness" (Chānd. VII.24). From the aforementioned and other scriptural passages, [it is established that the Lord possesses] attributes such as:
(1) resting in His own greatness, and (2) being the cause of...
Since the creation of the universe and so forth, as well as being the self of all objects, are determined to belong to the Supreme Person,
the term *bhūman* refers to the Supreme Person.
The Imperishable (is Brahman), because it supports that which is the limit of space.
(ether). The scriptural text says thus: "O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas call that the Indestructible (Akṣara). It is neither gross, nor..."

"of the size of an atom" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8). Here, that which is denoted by the term "Indestructible" is the Supreme Brahman, because He is said to be the support of that which is the ultimate goal (or the locus).
[The merging] of ether. The scriptural passage beginning with "O Gārgī, that which is above the sky" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.7)— omitted in A 1.8— mentions [this].

In the third quarter (pāda) of the first chapter, regarding the ether (ākāśa) designated as the substratum of all modifications, when it is asked, "Upon what is that [ether] woven across and lengthwise?", the answer is given: "This indeed is that Imperishable (akṣara). Thus, the Imperishable is the substratum of all modifications, because it supports everything from air up to the sky.
Indeed, this space is the Pradhāna, the cause of wind, the ego, and the ether; that which sustains it is the Supreme Brahman.
And that [is so] because of the command. 10.

And that steadfastness is heard in scripture as being performed under the supreme command of this Imperishable, according to the passage beginning with, "O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable. Therefore, the meaning is that this Imperishable is neither the individual soul nor the material cause.
Space (*ākāśa*) is the support of all changing things. Again, it is asked: "In whom is this space woven crosswise and lengthwise? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.7). In answering the above question:

The text—"This is the Imperishable (Akṣara)" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8)—states that the Akṣara is the support of that which is at the end of Āmbara (ether), which is contained within Vāyu (wind). The purport of this is as follows: [text continues]
The entire point is this: that space (ākāśa),
which is said to be the support of all mutable things, is identical with the *pradhāna* or the *avyakta*, the primordial cause and the place of dissolution of the ether (*ambara*).
[The ether] pregnant with wind. That which is called the Imperishable (akṣara), the support of the Pradhāna,
is the Supreme Brahman.
10. *Sa ca praśāsanāt*. And that [support] arises from command. Such a form of support is said to have originated from [the Lord's] command.
Furthermore, in the text, "O Gārgī! That which is above the supreme command of the Imperishable... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9), it is stated that [the Imperishable] is the supreme command.
Therefore, this Imperishable cannot be the individual self either.
Vedāntasāra: And because of the exclusion of other states of being. (11)

"Being other than something else" means "otherness. For the remainder of the passage, beginning with "The unseen Seer," excludes this Imperishable from being anything other than the Supreme Self. Therefore, it is the Supreme alone. [Adhikaraṇa]
Section 4: The Topic of the Object of Beholding.
Sūtra 12: He [is Brahman], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of beholding.

Furthermore, beginning with the passage, "But he who meditates on that Supreme Person by means of this very syllable 'Om' consisting of three measures," and continuing until, "He beholds the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the highest, beyond this mass of living beings," [it is established that the object of meditation is Brahman]. (11) And because there is an exclusion of any other state of existence.
And because of the negation of being other than that [the Highest Self].
"Being other" means "being different. Furthermore...
The portion of the sentence, "The unseen seer, the unheard hearer," negates the difference between the Imperishable (akṣara) and the Supreme Self;
therefore, it is the Supreme One alone.
He (the Highest Self) is the object of seeing,
because of the declaration of His essential character.
characteristics.
The scriptural passage beginning with "But he who meditates with this syllable Om, consisting of three mātrās, upon... [continues].

The meaning is that the object of the act of seeing preceded by meditation— described as the "Highest Person" and concluding with "he sees the Person dwelling in the citadel, higher than the high"— is the Supreme Self, the Ruler. This is further confirmed later by the passage beginning, "He [attains] the Imperishable through the syllable Om..."

This is because of the designation of attributes unique to the Supreme Person: "The wise man follows it through the thread [of the Upanishads], which is peaceful, undecaying, immortal, fearless, and supreme"; and also because of the designation that its abode is visible to the seers (sūri): "That which the poets know."
Section on the Small One (Daharādhikaraṇa) 5: The Small One [is Brahman], because of the subsequent [scriptural] passages. 13.
"Now, in this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-shaped dwelling; within it is a small space (ākāśa).
That which is within that [space] is what one must seek, and that indeed is what one must desire to understand. In this passage, the object of [inquiry] is the small [space].
The perception preceded by meditation is that Ruler, the Supreme Self. In the subsequent passage, it is stated thus:
"By means of the syllable Om, the wise one attains Him who is..."

"tranquil, undecaying, immortal, and fearless" (Pras. V-7). These are mentioned as the attributes peculiar to the Highest Self. Furthermore, it is because in the scriptural text, "The wise sages... [it is so stated].
In the passage, "Know Him," it has been pointed out that the seers behold His abode (namely, heaven).
13. *Dahara uttarebhyaḥ* (The small [ether] is [Brahman], because of the subsequent [arguments]).
The subtle [ether] is Brahman, because of the subsequent statements.
The scriptural passage, "Now, that which is within this city... [continues].
Brahman is a dwelling-place, a small lotus-flower. Within it is a small space. That which is within that should be sought;
indeed, that is what one should desire to know (Chāndogya Upaniṣad).
Vedāntasāra:
[Adhikaraṇa 1] The Supreme Self is indicated by the word "ether" (kāśa), on account of the qualities peculiar to it found in the subsequent passages.

Later on, having described the extreme vastness of the small ether (*daharākāśa*) by virtue of its being the support of all, and having pointed it out with the words, "This is the true city of Brahman," and having stated that desires are contained within this small ether known as the city of Brahman,
when the inquiry arises as to what this small ether is and what those desires are, [the text says]: "This is the Self..."

By beginning with "one whose evil has been struck down" and ending with "whose desires are true and whose resolve is true," [the text] makes it known that the Self is the small ether (daharākāśa), and that qualities such as being free from evil are its specific attributes.
In the passage, "Within this is a small ether; that which is within it is what one must seek," regarding this small ether—
It is understood that it has been stated that both that which exists within the city and that [which is outside] are to be sought after;
for it is revealed here: "Having discovered the Self and these true desires, they depart."
Now,
[the text] mentions the subtle ether (VIII.1.1). This subtle ether is the Highest Self, because of its specific attributes.

frequently mentioned. In the subsequent passage, the subtle ether (ākāśa) is said to be the support of all the worlds and is therefore described as being of immense magnitude. Furthermore, it is subsequently stated that...

The city mentioned above is identical with the Brahman that is Truth; and within that city of Brahman, which is the subtle ether (*ākāśa*), there exist various desires (desirable attributes). Then there are...

Inquiries were made as to what this subtle ether is and what those desirable attributes are. Then the following passage begins the answer, starting with "That is the Self, free from evil" and ending with...
"Whose wishes and purposes come true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.5).
Here, the subtle ether is the Highest Self. The desirable attributes are His freedom from evil and so forth.
In the passage,
"Within that is a small space. That which is within that should be sought" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1), the subtle ether and...
The contents therein are clearly stated to be sought after; this fact has been clearly indicated in the scriptural text: "Those who reach the highest place by meditating upon Him... and so forth.
"His true qualities" (Chānd. 8.1.6). First Chapter, Third Section: "On account of the path and the word; for thus it is seen [in scripture], and there is an indicative mark. (Sūtra 14)

"In this very way, all these creatures go day after day to this world of Brahman, yet they do not find it"— this refers to the daily departure of all creatures who, being ignorant, proceed above the small ether (daharākāśa).

The term *vartanam* (abiding) [is one indicator], and the word *brahmaloka* (the world of Brahman), which is used in grammatical apposition with the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*), makes it known that this small ether is the Supreme Brahman. For elsewhere, the abiding of all creatures upon the Supreme Self is observed in such passages as, "In Him all worlds are supported," and "The creatures [rest] in that supreme Imperishable. Brahman—
And there is the word *loka*, as in passages such as "This is the world of Brahman" (*eṣa brahmalokaḥ*). Even though [the term] is not seen elsewhere, this very [word] [is used here].
(14) Because of the movement upward and because of the indicative marks; for thus it is seen and there are signs.
The word [is the authority], for it is thus observed, and there is an inferential mark:
"In just this way, all these people go to this world of Brahman."
"Every day, but they do not know Him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.2).
This scriptural text states that every day all people, not knowing Him, move above the subtle ether; that is, they...
Rest upon Him. The term *brahma-loka* is used in grammatical apposition with the *ābhāsa* (manifestation) of the subtle form.
These two aforementioned facts assist in determining [the nature of the state].

That the subtle ether mentioned here refers to the Highest Brahman. In the following scriptural passages as well, it is observed that all beings find their rest in the Highest Self: "All... [rest] in Him."
"These worlds rest upon Him" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad II.6.1);
"People rest upon the highest Imperishable" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad II.1.3).
The term "Brahma-loka" is employed to signify the Supreme Person.
Regarding the scriptural passage, "This is the world of Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad IV.3.32),
we need not seek any other external reference to prove this fact.
[The term] *vartamānatvam* refers to its being present.
Vedāntasāra:
[Adhikaraṇa] There is sufficient evidence for this [Self] being the Supreme Self, namely, that it exists above the limited space (daharākāśa) as the Brahmaloka.
And sound [is also impermanent].
And because its greatness is perceived in this [earth] through the word "ghṛta. (15)
Now, because the greatness of the Supreme Self— the support of the universe—

is perceived in this small ether (daharākāśa) through the statement, "That which is the Self is the bridge, the supporter," this [ether] is the Supreme. For that greatness of the Supreme Self is described in such scriptural passages as, "He is the bridge, the supporter."
And because of common renown. || 16 ||
The aforementioned proofs alone— namely, that all people rest upon the subtle ether (ākāśa) and the usage of the term "Brahma-loka"— are sufficient to establish this.
15. And because the qualities such as supporting and so forth, which determine its greatness, are perceived in this [earth].
Brahman are perceived in It.
That He is the support of the world is established by the scriptural text: "Now, that which is the Self is the bank..."
"the limiting support" (Chānd. VIII.4.1). Within this subtle ether, there are perceived those qualities which determine the greatness of the Supreme Self, the support of the world.
The qualities that determine the greatness of the Highest Self are stated in the scriptural text: "He is the bank and support," and so forth (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad IV.4.22).
16. And because its meaning is established [in the scriptural texts].
Because the word *ākāśa* is well-known to refer to the Supreme Self— as in the passage, "That which is this bliss in the *ākāśa*"—

and because it is augmented by a multitude of qualities such as "truthful resolve" (*satyasaṃkalpa*), this [term] refers to the Supreme; whereas its application to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) is merely conventional.
The meaning is that common usage is more powerful.
If it be argued that he [is the one referred to] because of the reference to the other, we say no, because of impossibility. (Sūtra 17)

If it is argued that the ether under discussion is the individual soul (jīva), because of the reference to "that serene being" (*atha ya eṣa saṃprasādaḥ*) as the other [subject], this is not so; for the qualities previously mentioned are impossible in that case.
But if [the opponent] says "the subsequent," [we reply: it is indeed one whose true nature has become manifest. || 18 ||
The word *ākāśa* has been determined to signify the Supreme Self in the scriptural text: "This *ākāśa* which is bliss... (Tait. Up. 2.7.1). Therefore, it refers to the Supreme Self.
Therefore, the term *ākāśa* is more commonly used to denote the Highest Self, which possesses qualities such as the power of true resolve, than it is to denote the elemental ether.
17. If it be argued that "he" refers to the individual soul because of a reference to the other [the Supreme Self], we say no, because of impossibility.
Answer: No, because of impossibility.
If it be argued that the individual self is referred to in the scriptural text: "Now, he who is the *saṃprasāda*... [and so forth].
(Chānd. VIII-3-4), and therefore this word *ākāśa* refers to the individual self; this is not so, for the qualities mentioned therein are impossible in the individual self.
18. If it be argued that [the individual soul is meant] because its true nature is revealed by a subsequent passage; rather, [the Supreme Self is meant].
...the Self (ātman) insofar as its true nature has become manifest,
[possessing qualities] such as the realization of true intentions (*satyasaṃkalpa*), etc., M. 1.2 [adhikaraṇa].

In the Vedāntasāra, it is stated further on that because the individual soul (jīva) is heard of as having its impurities destroyed and so forth in the passage, "That Self which is free from evil," there is no impossibility [of its being Brahman]; for it exists throughout the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so on. Indeed, he...

If it is argued that he is the individual soul (jīva), this is not so; for his true nature has become manifest. Previously, through connection with a body commenced by karma, his qualities such as being free from sin were concealed; subsequently, having attained union with the supreme light, his true nature becomes manifest therein.

The individual soul (jīva) has been established as possessing qualities such as having evil destroyed; however, the small ether (daharākāśa) is an ocean of unobscured auspicious qualities, and thus it is not this individual soul.
And the reference has another purpose. (Sūtra 19)
In a subsequent passage, the statement occurs:
"This Self, free from evil" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad VIII.7.1). This passage refers to the individual self; therefore, there is no possibility whatsoever [of it being the Supreme Self].

They do not arise here. Indeed, it is certainly the individual self (jīva) that is referred to in this context, since it undergoes the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth. This is not so; [the reference is] to the state...
The mind relates to the individual self whose true nature has become manifest. Qualities such as "freedom from evil" and so forth are concealed by association with the bodies.
are the products of *karman* (past actions). Subsequently, when they reach the Supreme Light,
then their true nature becomes manifest and they—
possesses qualities such as "freedom from evil" and so forth. Such an individual self (jīva) is mentioned in the aforementioned text. However, the *ākāśa* of the subtle form is mentioned as...
An ocean of manifold auspicious qualities,
it can never be concealed; therefore, the term *ākāśa* does not refer to the individual self (*jīva*).
And that which is referred to here has a different purpose.
1. Being concealed by its association [with the body], [the Self is revealed]—in the third quarter of the first chapter (A 2, M 1):

“Having risen from this body and having attained the highest light, he manifests in his own form. This refers to the manifestation of the true nature of the individual self (*jīvātman*) through its attainment of the inner space (*daharākāśa*).
In this context, the reference to the individual soul (jīva) is for the purpose of demonstrating its greatness.
If it be argued that [the term] refers to one of little learning, that has already been answered. || 20 ||
If it is argued that this is not the Supreme Self because of scriptural statements regarding its smallness of abode and smallness of nature, the answer to that has been stated:
"Because it is to be perceived as such, and like the ether."
And because of the imitation of that. || 21 ||
"The individual self, having departed from this body, reaches the highest light and regains its own form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad VIII.3.4).
The aforementioned text states that the individual self...
When he reaches the *daharākāśa* (the subtle ether), he regains his own true nature. Thus, the text mentions the *jīva* solely for the purpose of explaining the power of the Highest Self.
Granting the individual self its essential nature.
20. *Alpaśruter iti cet tad uktam*. If it be argued that the scriptures declare [the contrary], that has already been answered.
"Small"; this objection has already been answered.
This is not the Highest Self, because the scriptures declare that He occupies a small space and that by His very nature He is exceedingly minute.
small. To this, the answer has already been given:
because Brahman must be meditated upon in that manner, and because in that very same passage Brahman is described as such.
"like ether" (Sūtra 1.2.7).

And because of the imitation of that [Supreme].
The self by means of the individual self. Furthermore,
because there is scriptural mention of the imitation of that supreme light by the small ether (daharākāśa), it is not [the self] of the individual soul (jīva).

The individual soul (jīva) is the small ether (daharākāśa). From such passages as, "There he moves about, eating, playing, and rejoicing," it is heard that through attaining union with that [ether], there occurs an imitation of it in the form of independent activity.
And he smiles. || 22 ||
Thus [it is said].
*Vedāntasāra*:
"Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature;
even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer."
Topic 6:
He is known from the word alone. (Sūtra 23)
The individual self is said to imitate the Supreme Light, which is the subtle ether (*ākāśa*); therefore,
the individual self is not the subtle ether.
Question: Consider the scriptural text, "There he approaches Him, eating, playing, and rejoicing" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3). Here it is stated that, having approached Him, he imitates Him.
Acting according to his desire.
22. *Api smaryate*: This is also declared by the *smṛti*.
It is stated in the Smṛti as follows: "Those who take refuge in this knowledge and attain the possession of the qualities that characterize Me, are neither born at the time of creation, nor..."
"are afflicted at the time of dissolution" (Bhagavad Gītā XIV.2).
23. Sabda-deva-pramitah: The "Measured One" is the Supreme Self, because of...

The term itself [indicates this], because of the hearing of a resemblance: "A person the size of a thumb dwells in the middle of the self, the ruler of beings... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.13). A 1.3.24. The first chapter, third quarter. A person the size of a thumb dwells in the middle of the self; he is the ruler of beings...
In such passages as these, the Supreme Self is measured by the thumb, precisely because of the scriptural statement regarding His sovereignty over all: "The Ruler of what has been and what is to be."
But with respect to the heart of one who is capable [of liberation], [the qualification belongs] to humans, because [the teaching] has humans as its primary authority. || 24 ||

Although [the Lord] is unlimited, his measurement as being the size of a thumb is stated with reference to his abiding within the heart of a worshiper. Since worship is possible only for humans, and since the scripture has them as its intended audience, this is said with reference to the human heart.
This point remains established and will be concluded later.
The Section Concerning the Deities (Devatādhikaraṇa) 7:
"Above that [the world of Brahman] as well, Bādarāyaṇa [maintains it is possible], because of the possibility. (Sūtra 25)
"The person the size of a thumb resides in the center of the self as the lord of the past and the future" (Katha Upaniṣad II.4.12).
Here, the one who is mentioned as being measured by the size of a thumb—

It is the Highest Self, because of the use of the words "His Lordship" and "the Lord of the past and the future. 24. But with reference to the heart, [the mention of the size of a thumb] is due to the fact that human beings are the qualified subjects.
But the reference is to the heart, because men are qualified [to meditate upon the Brahman].
Even the Infinite One is mentioned as being measured by it.
The size of the thumb, because He resides in the hearts of men who meditate upon Him. Only men are entitled to meditate upon Him; the scriptures are intended for men. Therefore, this...
This is stated with reference to the hearts of men. This topic will be concluded later on. Men...
25. Taduparyapi bādarāyaṇaḥ saṃbhavāt; Bādarāyaṇa thinks that even those who are above [the gods] meditate upon Him, because it is possible. (Vedāntasāra)
[Adhikaraṇa:

The venerable Bādarāyaṇa held that the meditation on that Brahman exists even among the gods and others, because the possibility of desire and capability exists for them; and this possibility arises from the non-forgetting of knowledge acquired in previous lives, as evidenced by the mantras and arthavādas.

Because praise is seen [in scripture] as having a body and so forth, for the sake of establishing that, and because they possess a body and so forth through the authority of those very [scriptures], their existence is established.
If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe multiple ways of attaining [liberation]. || 26 ||

If it is argued that there is a contradiction regarding action because it is impossible for a single [entity] possessing a body and so forth to be simultaneously present in multiple places; we say no, because we observe the simultaneous assumption of multiple bodies by those possessed of power, such as Saubhari and others.
The illustrious Bādarāyaṇa thinks thus:
even the gods, who are superior to humans, meditate upon that Brahman, for they too are regarded as supplicants. Such is the case.
It is possible for them, because they do not lose the memory of the knowledge they previously acquired. In the mantras and arthavādas of the Veda, the deities are praised as possessing—
Therefore, in order to justify that [the gods possess bodies],
one must accept the existence of the bodies of the gods on the authority of those very Vedic passages.
26. If it be argued that [the scripture] is contradicted with respect to ritual actions, we say no, because we observe various ways of attaining [the same result].
Consideration of the assumption of multiple bodies:
Suppose the gods possess bodies. In that case, a single individual deity could not be present simultaneously in all locations. Therefore, [the gods must be bodiless].
There arises a contradiction regarding ritual works;
this is not so, because it is observed that Saubhari and others assumed multiple bodies simultaneously.
If it is argued that [the world] arises from that [Veda], because it exists when that exists—just as Saubhari [arose] from his power—the third quarter of the first chapter states:
"If it be said that it is the Word (śabda), no; because the world originates from it, according to both perception and inference. (Sūtra 27)

But if it is argued that a contradiction arises regarding Vedic words—namely, that because the body possesses parts and is subject to origination, and since the gods such as Indra originate before [the word] and perish after, the Vedic words for Indra and others would either be devoid of referents or be non-eternal; [we reply]: no, because they originate from this [Veda]. The Vedic words for Devendra and the other gods—

[This is] because of the creation of Indra and others for that purpose. For words such as "Indra" do not denote individuals; rather, like words such as "cow," they denote generic forms (*ākṛti*). When a previous Indra or similar being has perished, Brahmā, by means of the very Vedic word "Indra" and so forth, recollects the specific form of the former Indra and the like, and [creates] another Indra of that same shape, just as a potter [creates a new pot].
27. If it be argued that [a contradiction arises] because of the word, we say no, because [the world] originates from That, as established by perception and inference.

To this he says:

8. Camasavadaviśeṣāt: Because there is no mention of a specific distinction, as in the case of the *camasa* (cup).

A *camasa* is a cup used in the sacrifice for drinking Soma juice. In the passage, "The one unborn [goat], red, white, and black, producing many offspring," the *prakṛti* (primordial matter) established in the Tantras is not stated to be the cause; for she is not [the cause] merely by virtue of being connected with the absence of birth.
Such an understanding arises because, in the absence of a specific indicator within the context, it is like the statement, "The cup has its mouth below.

For instance, in the passage "This is that head," the cup is specifically identified; indeed, the cognition of a specific distinction arising from an etymological word depends upon a specific indicator.
But [the soul] has light as its starting point, for so it is studied by some.

Brahman is light. This unborn one, whose source is light, has Brahman as her cause. For instance, the scriptural text: "The unborn one, red, white, and black, who gives birth to many creatures" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5), does not...

It is stated that the *prakṛti* of the Sāṃkhyas is the cause of the creation and so forth of the world. It cannot be said that, upon considering the secondary sense— namely, the absence of birth— [the term "unborn" refers to the Lord].

In this context, *prakṛti* alone is understood, because the word *ajā* has not been used here with any specific technical meaning, unlike the word *camasa* in the scriptural passage: "The *camasa*..."

"with downward-turned mouth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad II.2.3). Here, the word *camasa* is used in a specialized sense. The scriptural passage supporting this is: "It is the head" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad II.2.3).
The apprehension of a specific entity by means of a derivative word is due to the mention of its qualifying attributes.

Brahman as its cause. The text begins with, "Smaller than the small, greater than the great," etc. (Tait.

10. And because of the teaching of *kalpanā* (creation), there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth.
Regarding the Madhuvidyā, the term ‘kalpanā’ means ‘creation’. This is stated in the scriptural text: "The Creator created the sun and the moon."

"They were before" (Tait. II.1.38). Furthermore, the creation of *prakṛti* has been taught in the text: "The Lord of wondrous power created this universe from this" (Śvet. IV.9). Therefore, [there is no...]

A contradiction arises regarding the Pradhāna’s being unborn and [its] being the effect of Brahman. And there is no contradiction because, at the time of dissolution, even insentient matter abandons name and form.

Its state of being unborn (*ajatvam*) consists in its abiding in the form of Brahman as a subtle essence. At the time of creation, Prakṛti assumes names and forms and has Brahman as its cause. Just as at the time of creation, the sun possesses the nature of honey and the state of being an effect by virtue of being the substratum for the flavors to be enjoyed by the Vasus and others; likewise, at the time of dissolution, that very same [sun] exists in a subtle form that is no longer fit for designations such as "honey."
And in the Madhu-vidyā, the prohibition of [certain] actions is perceived: "Yonder sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods...

Being produced by Brahman, insentient beings,

that stage. At the time of creation, they assume name and form;

At the time of the dissolution of the flood, it assumes a subtle form that cannot be designated as "honey" (madhu), nor does it assume the state of being an effect. The scriptural passages supporting this are as follows:

“He, on whom the five [sets of] five things, etc. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad IV.4.17).

Beyond the twenty-five categories. The referents of the words "He" and "ākāśa" are distinct from the twenty-five varieties of *prakṛti*. Even the word used in [the phrase] "from... [is so].

This is understood from the supplementary passage beginning with "the eye of the eye. Because they are mentioned in conjunction with the eye and the ear, the terms *prāṇa* and *anna* also refer to the sense organs of touch and the rest, respectively.

Among the categories of effects such as space and the rest, in all Vedānta passages where the cause is not specifically determined—such as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" and "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated"—it is stated:

Since it is specifically that which is designated by a statement expressing a particularity that is spoken of, there is no consequence of falling into the causal theories of the Tantras, such as those concerning the unmanifest (avyākṛta) and so forth.
