But on account of scripture, because [the matter] has its root in the Word. || 27 ||

This consequence does not arise because the authority rests solely on the Śruti. Since the nature of Brahman has verbal testimony as its sole means of knowledge, and since it is of a different class from any object known through all other means of knowledge, it is not contradictory for Brahman to possess powers not observed elsewhere.
Therefore, it is possible for that which is perfect to exist simultaneously as both effect and cause, just as in the case of a genus.
Among disputants, [the term "cow"] arises with respect to things such as the hornless and the horned.
If Brahman were to assume the state of being an effect,
the scriptural statement that "Brahman is without parts" would become enraged— that is, it would be contradicted. Therefore, Brahman is not [the effect].
This [view regarding] the cause of the creation and so forth of the world has been refuted as follows: "But because of the Veda being the source of the word. (Sūtra 27).
But this is not so, on account of the authority of scripture; for the nature of Brahman can be apprehended solely through verbal testimony.

This objection does not arise, for the scriptures have been accepted as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The nature of Brahman can be established only through the authority of the scriptures. Brahman is...
Since it is distinct from other objects that could be established by other means of proof, no contradiction arises if Brahman possesses powers not seen in other objects.

Therefore, the conclusion is this: Brahman is in every respect fully endowed with all attributes, both in its causal state and in its effected state. This is just as [the view] of those who accept *jāti* (universal).
It is a separate category [of sin], and it is fully present in each of the cows that have broken horns or are hornless.
— Vedāntasāra:
And it is the same with respect to the self; for [the results] are indeed diverse. || 28 ||
Furthermore, the connection of the individual self (jīvātman) with attributes that are contrary to non-sentient properties arises precisely because it possesses powers of an entirely different kind.
Even specific non-sentient entities such as fire and water are seen to be mutually distinct, possessing fixed powers and diverse characteristics.
[Adhikaraṇa: And the faults of one’s own position. || 29 ||
Since defects such as the consequence of total pervasion apply only to the partless *pradhāna*, which is of the same nature as non-intelligence (*acit*), Brahman alone is the cause.
28. And likewise in the Self; for there are diverse powers.
The individual self possesses attributes that are contrary to those residing in insentient beings; this is due to the specific powers inherent in it. Insentient beings...
For instance, fire, water, and so forth, possess mutually contradictory attributes, are endowed with specific powers inherent to them, and are observed to be distinct from one another.
29. And on account of the defects of his own views as well.
Defects such as the whole transforming itself into the effect exist only in the case of the *pradhāna*,
which is partless and of the same class as the non-sentient.
Therefore, Brahman is the cause of the creation and so forth of the world. Second Chapter, First Section:
"And [Brahman] is endowed with all [powers], because that is seen [in scripture]. (Sūtra 30)
And from the Vedic scripture, "His power is heard to be indeed manifold," it is understood that the deity is endowed with all powers.
If it is argued that [the Lord] is not [the cause] because He is devoid of instruments, that has already been answered. || 31 ||

If it is argued that Brahman cannot be the cause because it is devoid of organs— as stated in the text, "For him there exists neither activity nor organ"— the answer to this is precisely what was stated in the preceding sūtra: that [Brahman's causality] is possible because it is of a different nature [from ordinary agents], being based solely on the authority of scripture.
30. And that deity is endowed with all [powers],
because it is seen as such in the scriptures.
The divinity is apprehended as being endowed with all powers in the scriptural text: "His high power is manifested as manifold," and so forth (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad VI.8).
31. "If it be argued that [the Lord] is not [the agent] because He is devoid of organs, this has already been answered. This question was previously resolved.
Brahman is not the cause of the creation and so forth of the world, because He is devoid of sense organs. This is stated in the scriptural text: "Neither His body nor His sense organ is perceived."

"Exist" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad VI.8). To this, the reply is as follows: In a previous sūtra (II.1.27), it was stated that the nature of Brahman can be established solely through the means of scripture.
He is distinct from all other objects.
(Vedāntasāra: Section 10, on the Possession of Purpose)
• Not so, because it possesses a purpose. || 32 ||
Since Brahman has all its desires fulfilled, there is no purpose for creation; therefore, Brahman is not the cause.
[Adhikaraṇa 12] But like the world, His play is His sole motive. (33)

Even for one who has attained all desires, independence is possible when [the world] is for the purpose of sport (*līlā*), since in the world we observe the undertaking of games like ball-throwing and the like for the sake of mere sport alone. For this Self-satisfied One, there is no [need for the world] because all desires have been attained; thus, it is not [the case that He acts] for the sake of a purpose. (32) *Na prayojanavattvāt* (Not on account of having a purpose).
Brahman is not the cause because the world has the nature of being dependent upon a motive.
Brahman has all his desires fulfilled; therefore...

There is no purpose in creating the world; therefore, Brahman is not the cause of the creation and so forth of the world. 33. But as in the case of the world, [Brahman's activity is] mere sport (līlā) and isolation (kaivalya).
But it is merely sport, as in ordinary worldly life.
Regarding the creation of the world, sport may well be the motive, even though His every wish is already fulfilled. Therefore, it is...

It is appropriate to say that He does not expect to gain anything from the creation and so forth of the world. In ordinary life, balls and such are used in games merely for sport; in His case, it is likewise.

For one who is self-satisfied, "the fulfillment of all wishes" means that there is no purpose for creation; [for] if creation were the purpose of divine play (*līlā*), [it would follow that the Lord is not self-sufficient].
[The author] is authoritative because his desires have been fulfilled.
[End of] the first quarter of the second chapter.
For there is always the presence of all desired objects of enjoyment and instruments [of pleasure]. The satisfaction derived from enjoyment is of a different genus from the satisfaction of the Self;
even the essence of divine play (līlā-rasa), which is distinct from that, has as its very instruments the three guṇas, the Puruṣa, and so forth.
There is no partiality or cruelty [on the part of the Lord], because He has regard for [other factors]; for thus Scripture shows. || 34 ||

Partiality and cruelty do not apply to the Supreme Being on account of His unequal creation of gods and others, because that unequal creation depends upon the karma of the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*). Thus, the Śruti itself demonstrates this: "The doer of good becomes good; the doer of evil becomes evil."
The readiness of all necessaries essential for the enjoyment of all pleasures at all times. The satisfaction derived from the enjoyment of pleasures is distinct from the Self.
Satisfaction. The relish in sport is distinct from the two kinds of satisfaction mentioned above. Both *pradhāna* and the individual self (*jīva*) are necessary requisites for His sport.
34. There is no inequality or cruelty [on the part of Brahman], because it is dependent on other factors; for thus [the scripture] shows.
In the portion concerning Brahman, there is neither...
Neither inequality nor cruelty [can be attributed to Him], because He acts with a specific purpose; for thus the scriptures declare.
While creating the gods and others of diverse status, [He does so]...
Since he is compassionate toward all living beings, he is neither partial nor cruel by nature.
The inequality in creation by the Supreme Self is due to the *karmas* or deeds of the individual selves. This is observed in...
Thus says the scriptural text: "He who performs good deeds becomes good; he who performs evil deeds becomes evil" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad IV.4.5).
Because it is dependent upon the field, the agent, and karma (M 3.1),
the adjunct (*upādhi*) is indeed eternal (A1,
M1). Vedāntasāra.

If it be argued that [the distinction between the individual soul and Brahman] does not exist because there is no differentiation of karma, we say: no; for it is justified by the beginninglessness [of saṃsāra], and it is both logically established and perceived. || 35 ||

If it is argued that because of the restriction to oneness in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only," there can be no action at that time due to the absence of individual souls (*kṣetrajña*), we say: no; for the individual souls are beginningless, and their respective actions—

And there is indeed a continuous flow (pravāha). Furthermore, even if that [flow] is beginningless, the scriptural statement regarding non-distinction (*avibhāga*) is appropriate, because of the absence of the distinction between name and form (*nāmarūpa-vibhāga*); for this is consistent with the meaning of the passage: "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated; it was differentiated by name and form. Moreover, the beginninglessness of the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) is perceived in the scriptures: "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower..."
Regarding Śanīśa: "The eternal among the eternals."
35. If it be argued that there are no actions because of [the absence of] a prior limit, we say: no, for they are established by their beginninglessness, and they are also perceived.
[Objection: There is a difference [between the two]. [Reply: We say, "Not so, because of beginninglessness";
this is logical and is also so observed.
Unity is apprehended in the scriptural text: "Being..."
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad VI.2.1). At that time, individual selves did not exist;
therefore, karmas or deeds do not adhere to it.
the individual selves. This is not so; since the individual selves are without beginning, the stream of their karmic actions is also without beginning. This is logical. The individual selves...
They have no beginning; yet the scriptural text stating their non-difference merely establishes their lack of distinction due to the absence of name and form. The text is as follows:
"Verily, at that time this world was undifferentiated. It became differentiated only by name and form" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7).
The aforementioned view is in harmony with this scriptural text.
And because all dharmas are possible [only] on the basis of the scriptural texts that establish the beginningless nature [of the world]. (2.1.36)

Since all phenomena— such as primordial matter (*pradhāna*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth— are untenable, and because Brahman is characterized by being distinct from everything else and possesses all powers according to scriptural testimony, it is established that Brahman alone is the cause.
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the Vedāntasāra composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
The individual selves are as follows: "The two unborn, the conscious and the unconscious, are the Lord and the non-Lord" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.9).
"He is the eternal among the eternal" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.13).
36. Sarvadharmopapatteśca: And because all attributes are proved to be present in Brahman.
All those attributes which are impossible in the *pradhāna* and the atoms are found in Brahman, because He is apprehended as distinct from all other objects. All.
His powers are established by the scriptures. Therefore, it is proven that Brahman alone is the cause of the creation and so forth of the world.

Thus ends the second quarter (pāda) of the second chapter (adhyāya). The second quarter of the second chapter: Topic 1: The Non-establishment of the World’s Structure. Sūtra 1: And because the structure [of the world] is impossible [if derived from atoms], and because of [the nature of] activity, there is no [validity for] inference [regarding a creator].

Furthermore, since the construction of chariots, palaces, and the like from wood and other materials is impossible for those who lack knowledge of them unless they are supervised by someone possessing such knowledge—

and since the activity of construction proceeds only when supervised by one who knows— it follows that the Pradhāna, being insentient, is not the cause of the world unless it is supervised by an intelligent being. Thus, the Pradhāna is known through inference [to be non-causal].
1. And because the formation [of the world] is impossible, there is no inference [of Pradhāna as the cause], and because of the activity [of the Lord].
The inference [of Pradhāna] is not the cause of the creation and so forth of the world, because of its impossibility.
[It is established] by way of the possibility of construction and by way of activity.
The construction of chariots, mansions, and so forth cannot be accomplished by insentient things such as wood.
...and so forth, [these things] would not exist without being employed by a person who knows how to perform them; yet they can be produced when employed by such a person. Therefore, the...
Pradhāna— that which is insentient, provable solely through inference, and not directed by an intelligent agent— cannot be the cause of the creation and so forth of the world.
And likewise in that case [of the soul's departure], as in the case of milk and water, because of the knowledge of its nature. (M.S. 3.2.2)

If it is argued that "just as milk and water are independent [of other causes] in becoming curd and so forth, so too is the Pradhāna," the reason for this has already been refuted; for that too is included within the subject of the proposition.
Because there is no dependence on an indefinite succession of absences. || 3 ||
Furthermore, because it would entail the consequence of constant creation due to its independence from being presided over by an intelligent being, the Pradhāna is not the cause.
2. If it be argued that it is like milk or water, even in that case,
the wise guides [would respond].

Milk and water are not directed by an intelligent person when they undergo transformations such as curds and so forth; the same is the case with *prajñāna* (consciousness) as well. The answer is as follows: even...
In this case, the reason for reductio ad absurdum is the same as that already stated; for even milk and water are included within the subject (pakṣa).
And because of the non-establishment of the absence [of creation] due to the independence of Pradhāna,
there would never be a reversal of creation.
The world.
The *pradhāna* is not the cause of the creation and so forth of the world; otherwise, creation would occur at all times, since...
The guidance of an intelligent being is not required at all;
for even primordial matter (*pradhāna*) [acts] through independence.
[The cause is] omitted in M1, 2. [Adhikaraṇa:
Vedāntasāra:
And because of its non-existence elsewhere, it is not like grass and so forth. || 4 ||]

It is not correct to say that the *pradhāna* is like the grass and other things consumed by a cow when it becomes milk; for such a thing is not observed in the case of oxen and the like, since that [transformation] is presided over by an intelligent being (*prājña*).
If it is argued that [the soul] is like a person, even so, [it is not]. || 5 ||

If it is argued that the Puruṣa impels the Pradhāna by his mere proximity—like a blind man and a lame man, or like iron and a magnet—and thus there is no need for an intelligent overseer—we say: no; even so, the Pradhāna [cannot act] otherwise than [as directed], nor [can it act] like grass and such.
It is not like grass and so forth, because [the effect] does not arise from other things. It is not correct to say that *pradhāna* is the cause.

The creation and so forth of the world occur in the same manner as grass and other substances are capable of being transformed into milk when consumed by cows; for in the case of bulls and the like, such a transformation does not take place.
Since no such intelligence is observed [in these cases], the transformation of grass and other materials into milk and so forth must likewise be directed by an intelligent agent.
(5) If it is argued that this is like the case of a person, even so...
And if it is argued that it is like the case of the person and the stone, then likewise the Pradhāna cannot be the cause of the creation and so forth of the world.
The Self, through its mere presence, impels the Pradhāna to create the world. This is analogous to the case of a blind man led by a lame person. Another instance is the case of a...
The magnet-stone toward which the iron moves. Therefore, *kṣīrībhatraddhenū* (A 1, Pr.), *kṣīrabhāvidhenū* (M 2).
"Like a stone" (*aśmavat*) is added before; "and iron" (*ayaśca*) is omitted in M 2.
[The portion omitted in A I.1] The second quarter of the second chapter:
the impossibility of activity, because the Puruṣa is unchanging. [Activity such as] the instruction of a path and the journeying to another place belongs to the horse and so forth.
For there is indeed an occasional transformation.
And because the status of being the principal [the object] is untenable. || 6 ||

The evolution of the world proceeds from the state of secondary creation (*pratisarga*) through the relationship of predominance and subordination among the *guṇas* in their states of increase and decrease;

for in the state of equilibrium, since they exist in a condition of balance, the relationship of predominance and subordination produced by disequilibrium is impossible, and thus there would be no world.
The commencement.
It is not the case that the *pradhāna* does not require guidance by an intelligent self.
Even so, the *pradhāna* cannot be the cause of the creation and so forth of the world, because [it lacks] an intelligent person [to direct it].
It does not undergo any change. The lame man and the magnet undergo occasional changes by advising the path and moving from one place to another.
6. And because the status of being a member is untenable,
due to the impossibility of the predominance [of one] in relation to that which is predominant and subordinate.
It is systematic.
The origination of the world results from a specific relationship among the three *guṇas* as primary and subordinate.
This [distinction] depends upon the relative inferiority and superiority [of the qualities].
However, in the state of *pralaya*, the three *guṇas* exist in a state of equilibrium; therefore, none of them is superior or inferior to another.
Therefore, the creation of the world would not take place, [just as there is no creation] of things such as the binding of a fetter. (Prakaraṇapañcikā, Vedāntasāra 1.3)
And because of the absence of the power of cognition in the inference of Pradhāna by any other means.
(7) "The power of the cognizer"—because of the absence of that; the meaning is: because of the absence of the power of being a knower.
And in the inference of Pradhāna by a mode other than the one described, there is an absence of the power of being a knower in Pradhāna.
The defects, such as the impossibility of the world's creation and so forth, remain in the same state.
[Adhikaraṇa]:
Even if it were admitted [that there is a creator], it would not be so, because of the non-existence of an object. || 8 ||

Even if the Pradhāna is accepted, it cannot be inferred because there is no purpose [for its existence]. Furthermore, if the inference were made in another way, it would result in a separation from the capacity for knowledge, since the Puruṣa is changeless.
The result remains unchanged because the *pradhāna* is devoid of the power of cognition.
The expression "being devoid of the power of cognition" [is used].
The word *ing* means "being devoid of the capacity for intelligence.
Even if *pradhāna* were inferred by some reasoning other than that which has already been refuted by us, it would still be devoid [of such capacity].
The powers of knowing the difficulties, such as the impossibility of construction and so forth, mentioned in Sūtra II-2-1, remain firmly established.
8. Abhyupagamepyarthābhāvāt: Even if [the existence of the self] were admitted, it should not be inferred, because there is no purpose [for such an inference].
This is not to be inferred; for there would be no purpose served by considering *pradhāna* to be the cause of the world's creation and so forth. A wise person...

In the second quarter of the second chapter, it is shown that because modifications in the form of perception of the Pradhāna are impossible, neither experience— which is caused by the superimposition of the attributes of the material cause— nor liberation, which is produced by the sustained discernment of that [Pradhāna] from the Self, are possible.
And because of contradiction, [the Sāṃkhya doctrine] is inconsistent. || 9 ||
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya doctrine is inconsistent because it simultaneously accepts a thousand contradictory attributes of the Puruṣa, such as being a seer, an enjoyer, and immutable.
The Topic of the Great and the Long:
"Or rather, like the great and the long, [the effect arises] from the short and the spherical. (2.2.10)

It does not undergo any change, nor does it transform itself into the forms that *pradhāna* is capable of assuming. Therefore, these two things do not occur: (1) the experience [of pleasure and pain]; and...

(1) the bondage consisting of pleasure and so forth, which is caused by the superimposition of the attributes of *prakṛti* upon the intelligent self (*puruṣa*), and (2) the liberation that is attained through the discernment of oneself from those attributes.
[The Sāṃkhya doctrine is] inconsistent because of contradictions;
and [the same applies to] everything accepted regarding the Self.
It is not intelligible due to contradiction.
The doctrine of the Kāpilas is not intelligible, because of the acceptance of many contradictory attributes within the conscious principle.
The person [is inferred] from such qualities as the powers of seeing, enjoying, and non-modification, etc.
10. Or, like the large and long, [it is inferred] from the short and the circular.

And the views of others, such as those who accept the superimposition of the properties of *prakṛti* and experience caused by it: [as stated] in *Māṭhara-vṛtti* 1.2, "By the words 'large' (*mahat*) and 'long' (*dīrgha*), [the qualities of] the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) [are indicated]; by the word 'short' (*hrasva*), the triad (*tryaṇuka*); and by the word 'spherical' (*parimaṇḍala*), the atom (*paramāṇu*)."
The explanation:
*Vedāntasāra* [continues with] "it is inconsistent" (*asamañjasam*). The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "and. From the short and the spherical...

"Like the large and the long"; furthermore, their entire doctrine—such as the production of a triad from two dyads and atoms—is inconsistent. For parts, when joining by means of their six sides, indeed originate a larger composite whole; however, since atoms are partless, sides are not admitted, and thus [the production of a whole] does not depend upon sides.
For those things that are being conjoined, it is not possible for them to be the initiators of a substance [if they are already joined].
In either case, there is no action; therefore, that [action] does not exist. || 11 ||
The production of the large and the long from the short and the atom is untenable.
The term *asamañjasa* (untenable) is introduced here [from the preceding context].
The previous Sūtra. The word *va* (i.e., "or") is used in the sense of *ca* (i.e., "and"). The views of that school are completely unintelligible, which maintain the doctrine that the *tryaṇuka*...
That which is large and long is formed from *dvyaṇukas* (dyads) and *paramāṇus* (atoms). Generally, parts possessing six sides begin the formation of a larger object through their conjunction.
Atoms are partless; therefore, they cannot possess sides.
Entities such as atoms, when brought together regardless of their sides, cannot produce a large object.
11. In either case, there is no motion arising from atoms; therefore, there is no arising [of the world].
The world follows [this principle],
like the production of a dyad (vyaṇuka) and a triad (tryaṇuka); it is like the production of a triad and a pentad (paṇuka).
The possibility of the production of a substance [arises] from two paramāṇus, according to the Vaiśeṣika system of philosophy. M. 3. bhūbhṛtara M 2, Pr.
Atoms (also known as *parimaṇḍalas*) form a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), which is short in dimension. Three dyads form a triad (*tryaṇuka*), which is large and long.

"Because action inherent in the atom is impossible, there is an absence of conjunction with an atom caused by that [action]. Even though the unseen potencies (*adṛṣṭa*) of the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) depend upon their maturation, it is not possible for an occasional action inherent in an atom to be produced by them. If they were independent [of maturation], [the action] would have been produced even previously.
There would be water. "What is called ripening (*vipāka*) is not some unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) factor that arises;

rather, it is the very arrival at that specific time of that action for which the giving of its fruit was declared to be determined by a particular time at the moment of the performance of the action. For actions whose specific times are not determined, [the ripening occurs] due to other powerful actions—"
Maturation (*vipāka*) is indeed [the process of] obstruction. Furthermore, the unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) possess a nature that bestows fruits corresponding to their respective karmas.

Therefore, it is impossible for there to be a single, uniform maturation of deeds performed by infinite selves at various times, as they yield fruits at diverse times. Moreover, since a Lord who is to be inferred is unestablished, maturation cannot occur through His superintendence either.
It is impossible to accept that the first motion can originate within atoms. Therefore, the conjunction of two or more atoms cannot be accepted. Even if such a requirement were to exist...

Even if there were maturation of the *adṛṣṭa* (the unseen principle) within individual selves, nevertheless, occasional motion caused by that *adṛṣṭa* could not originate from atoms. Suppose [it were so]...

If maturity were not required, then the motion would have been produced in the atoms even prior to that. In fact, maturity is not produced anew as a specific attribute within the *adṛṣṭa*. When considered in this light...
According to the injunctions, specific actions yield specific results.
Then, at that particular time, the individual selves attain that fruit; this is called maturation (*vipāka*). When there is no specific...

The time for such fruits is fixed; their ripening consists in the state of not being obstructed by more powerful karmas. The unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) has the nature of bestowing those results which are dependent [on it].
the nature of the actions. Therefore, maturation does not find a fixed location in all individual selves simultaneously;
for various actions bestow various results at various [times].
The Lord cannot be established by means of inference;
therefore,
[it is so] because of the absence of conjunction (saṃyogābhāvāt).
"Because of that, there is arrival at that very time" (M3, Pr.).
M1 adds "ataḥ" before this.
Non-ripening is precisely the obstruction by another karma.
It is known from the Vedāntasāra [Avi. 1, 2, 3]. Pr. M. 1, 2, 3. It is known.
And because of the admission of inherence, there would be an infinite regress due to its being on the same footing [as the categories it connects]. 12.

Furthermore, [the Vaiśeṣika system] is inconsistent because of the postulation of inherence (*samavāya*); for, just as with universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth, inherence also requires a cause for its non-separate existence, leading to an infinite regress. If one were to imagine that inherence possesses that very nature [of non-separate existence], then it would be more appropriate to attribute that nature to the universal and the rest themselves.
And because it exists eternally. || 13 ||
If one accepts the eternality of inherence (*samavāya*), it would be untenable without the eternality of its relata;
consequently, both the part (*avayava*) and the whole (*avayavin*) would necessarily be eternal, and thus this [world] would be nothing but non-existent.
It is impossible to argue that atoms can create the world under the direction of the Lord. 12. And because of the admission of inherence, there would be an infinite regress.
And because, due to the admission of *samavāya*, an infinite regress results, owing to its being equal [to the other categories].
The views of the Vaiśeṣikas are also untenable, because they acknowledge *samavāya*; for *samavāya*,
like *jāti* (class) and *guṇa* (quality), likewise requires a substratum.
In order to prove the fact of its being inseparably connected, one must resort to another *samavāya*;
from this arises the fallacy of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is argued that this nature of *samavāya* is such that...
Since they are inseparably connected without requiring any other means of proof, let the same principle be applied to the cases of *jāti* and *guṇa* as well.
13. And it would be eternal; for in this way, both the part and the whole would be eternal due to its eternality.
Inherence (samavāya) is considered to be eternal. Such a consideration would not be possible without that [entity] to which the relation belongs.
Chapter 2, Section 2.
And because it possesses form and so forth, there is a reversal [of the nature of the soul], as seen from observation. || 14 ||
Furthermore, because atoms possess form and other qualities, they are subject to the opposite of permanence and so forth, since this is observed to be the case with jars and other such objects.
And because it would follow that there is no means [to avoid] the fault. || 15 ||

If atoms were devoid of color and other qualities due to the fear of impermanence and the like, then the principle that the quality of the effect is preceded by the quality of the cause would be unestablished. Conversely, if they possessed color and other qualities out of fear of those [faults], then impermanence and the like would follow; thus, because of these faults in both cases, [the theory] is simply untenable.
Since it is accepted as eternal, both the parts and the whole composed of those parts must likewise be eternal; therefore, this *samavāya* does not exist at all.

If it is asked, "What then is the meaning of the scriptural statement, 'He becomes a self-ruler' (*sa svarāḍ bhavati*)? For every resolve of the liberated soul is never [otherwise than fulfilled].
It is not obstructed by anything; even the Lord does not obstruct its resolve, because it never forms a resolve that is contrary to the will of the Lord.
